overview: The Ainu are an Indigenous people associated with Hokkaido, Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands and northern Honshu. These three map labels describe regional communities, not a single kingdom. The imported beginning at 4000 BCE and early outlines extending deep into Honshu conflate predecessor archaeology with later Ainu identity. The phases below distinguish that earlier background from medieval Ainu history; the map’s final date of 1715 does not mark the disappearance of Ainu people.

periods.title: Earlier regional archaeology
periods.summary: The map begins long before the formation of historically documented Ainu culture. Jomon and later archaeological remains belong to distinct earlier contexts.

periods.title: Satsumon and Okhotsk connections
periods.summary: Communities connected northern maritime routes with Honshu. Crops, ironworking and different house traditions contributed to later regional developments.

periods.title: Ainu culture and expanding exchange
periods.summary: Ainu culture developed around the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, at different times by region. Subsequent trade linked northern communities and Japanese merchants.

periods.title: Matsumae trading privileges
periods.summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu granted Matsumae exclusive trading rights in 1604. Commercial dependence created opportunities for coercion.

periods.title: Resistance and stronger outside control
periods.summary: Shakushain’s defeat strengthened Matsumae control. Ainu communities and regional traditions continued beyond the atlas endpoint.

items.text: Okhotsk communities reached Hokkaido from Sakhalin during the fifth century. Their coastal settlements supported fishing and marine hunting, with some pentagonal or hexagonal pit houses more than ten metres long. These are an earlier archaeological setting, rather than a description of every later Ainu household.

In eighth-century Satsumon settlements near river mouths, people combined salmon and trout fishing with wild plants, millet and barley cultivation. Square pit houses had cooking stoves. Iron tools and smithing skills arriving through exchanges with Honshu changed what people could make and repair.

Tenth-century Tobinitai pottery combines forms and decoration associated with Okhotsk and Satsumon traditions. Houses also show mixed features. Archaeologists can follow cultural exchange in a cooking pot as well as in a trade route.

An eighth-century pottery steamer from the Yura site at Iwamizawa had holes in its base and lower sides. Set above a water-filled pot, it let steam rise through cloth to cook grain. Its holes were useful kitchen engineering, not evidence that somebody had broken the bowl.

The steamer’s discovery has a school connection: in 1959, Sapporo West High School’s local-history club excavated a pit dwelling at Yura. Their find now helps museum researchers investigate how mainland cooking techniques reached Hokkaido more than a thousand years earlier.

Between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, above-ground dwellings increasingly replaced pit houses, while iron pots and traded lacquerware displaced locally made earthenware. Changes in trade were therefore changes at home too: a household’s cooking equipment could connect it to distant workshops.

Japanese-speaking Wajin traders established fortified dwellings called tate in southern Hokkaido. Their growing settlements brought exchange but also threats to Ainu livelihoods and armed conflict. The Kakizaki family, later named Matsumae, consolidated power among these settlers and obtained privileged access to Ainu trade.

Ainu traders exchanged salmon and animal pelts for rice, sake and iron goods. Rice entered meals and ceremonies, while Matsumae’s economy depended on the exchange. This was a relationship with valuable goods on both sides, although the domain increasingly imposed unfair terms to increase its profits.

Libation sticks called ikupasuy excavated beside the Miyanosawa River at Kaminokuni are dated to the late sixteenth or early seventeenth century. These small ritual objects give archaeologists a tangible connection with Ainu practices during the map’s later centuries.

In 1669, a dispute over fishing and hunting rights in Hidaka widened into Shakushain’s resistance against Matsumae oppression. Shakushain was killed at a feast celebrating a peace agreement. His defeat strengthened the domain’s hold; it did not erase Ainu communities or their knowledge.

At Tokoro, an Ainu chashi, or fort, occupied a river terrace near the sea around the early eighteenth century. The same archaeological complex also contains much older pit houses. University excavations distinguish these layers: sharing a hill does not make every building the same age.

sections.title: Later documented households, food and practical skills

items.text: Museum accounts of nineteenth- and early twentieth-century life describe houses with a central hearth and an entrance used for storage. Grass, reed screens and mats covered floors; some homes had low sleeping platforms. Materials and arrangements varied between regions and households.

Some households in these later accounts designated an outdoor rubbish area and separated hearth ash and rice bran from other waste. Nearby racks dried fish and meat, and rods held laundry. Keeping a home working required unglamorous jobs as well as skilled craftwork.

Later meals commonly combined soup and grain porridge. Wild plants, meat, fish or seaweed could enrich soup; food was dried and stored for winter shortages. Rataskep mixed vegetables, wild plants or beans with oil and salt. Preparation varied with local resources.

Fish could provide clothing as well as dinner. In documented later garments, pieces of salmon or trout skin were stitched into clothing with narrow sleeves and a wider hem. Other textiles used soft inner bark from elm or linden trees: the forest supplied fibres as well as firewood.

Hokkaido Museum restored a dwelling with guidance from Yaichiro Hama, born in Shiraoi in 1916. Its hearth warmed the earth while reed walls and roofing held in heat. The reconstruction records knowledge carried by a named person, including places for sleeping, sitting and keeping treasured objects.

A saranip basket could carry millet, gathered plants or fish. Makers combined tree bark and climbing-plant stems, changing the weave to make different shapes and sizes. The museum’s examples show a practical design problem familiar to any family: how to bring dinner home without dropping it.

Ainu oral literature includes heroic epics, mythic epics and prose tales. A mythic narrator might be an animal or another kamuy, a spiritual being. Such stories teach ways of behaving toward people and the living world; an entertaining tale could also carry serious lessons.

Chiri Yukie, who lived from 1903 to 1922, recorded and translated thirteen mythic epics. Her Ainu Shin’yoshu appeared in 1923 with Roman-letter Ainu and Japanese translations. It preserves a named Ainu author’s work, rather than treating oral tradition as anonymous material without its own interpreters.

A short writing sample from Chiri Yukie’s 1923 collection is “Shirokanipe ranran pishkan”: “Silver droplets fall all around.” It opens the owl spirit’s song. This is the book’s attested Roman-letter Ainu spelling, with an English rendering of its Japanese translation, not an inscription from the ancient map period.

In her preface dated March 1922, Chiri remembered storytelling gatherings on rainy evenings and snowy nights. She wanted readers to know her people through the words inherited from their ancestors. The preface turns a printed book into evidence of family and community transmission.

Ainu was traditionally transmitted through speech; later writers used Roman letters and katakana to record it. Upopoy explains that it is distinct from Japanese. The survival of recordings, books and learners makes language history an ongoing activity, not simply a display of old objects.

For present-day learners, Hokkaido Museum offers coloured blocks that assemble into Ainu sentences. Moving words and grammatical pieces around turns language structure into something a child can handle. These are modern teaching tools, showing one way museums support learning alongside books and performances.

After the Meiji government renamed Ezochi Hokkaido in 1869, settler expansion and state policies restricted Ainu language, customs, salmon fishing and deer hunting. Loss of land damaged the basis of family livelihoods. These nineteenth-century changes occurred long after the atlas’s 1715 endpoint.

A photograph from around 1930 records a poster advertising speeches by Ainu young people at Sapporo’s Clock Tower. The poster challenged Japanese prejudice and policies affecting Ainu people. Young people were publicly arguing about their future, not merely preserving memories of the past.

Living traditions include dance, embroidery, woodcarving and new music. Upopoy describes people recovering dances from older records while also creating new forms. Cultural continuity can involve both careful reconstruction and invention by today’s artists; it does not require every generation to live in the same kind of house.

ending.text: The map stops in 1715, but Ainu history continues through later coercion, resistance and cultural renewal. Ainu people remain living communities; the National Ainu Museum presents their language, work, exchanges and contemporary perspectives, rather than the remains of an extinct kingdom.
